definition: A dominant allele is a version of a gene whose effects are seen in an individual even when only one copy is present, as contrasted with a recessive allele. In the packet’s example, the dominant Tas1r3 allele is the one associated with the sweetener-related traits in the hybrid mice.

reasons: The definition’s general claim about what makes an allele “dominant” (effects seen with only one copy, contrasted with recessive) is not explicitly supported anywhere in the provided packet text.

The definition’s example claim is not supported: the packet attributes the observed behavioral/metabolic differences in 129S2B6−Tas1r3−/− F1 hybrids to expression of the recessive Tas1r3 allele, and it states that hemizygosity of Tas1r3 did not influence the relevant traits.
The packet does not support the specific phrasing that a “dominant Tas1r3 allele” is the one associated with the sweetener-related traits in the hybrid mice described.
The requested field is learning, but the term and source packet are about genetics/allelic variation rather than a learning concept, so the field is not defensible from the packet.
The definition adds a general claim that a dominant allele’s effects are seen when only one copy is present; the packet does not explicitly state this one-copy rule.

The example is loosely supported but overgeneralized: the packet says the C57BL/6J strain carries the dominant Tas1r3 allele, not that this allele is simply “the one associated with” all sweetener-related traits in hybrid mice.
